Sir,

The man mentioned in attached newspaper translation is
Matveef Bodroy who arrived here from Vladivostock on the 25th
ultimo by the S. S. "Nancy Moller". The latter steamer was
chartered by The Union of Siberian Co-Operative Unions, "Zakoo-
psbit", 12 Boone Road to take provisions to Nikolaevsk, but was
refused permission by the Japanese to enter this port. She
eventually discharged at Vladivostock. Matveef is well known
here as a Bolshevik and was connected with the Russian Employ-
ment Bureau which closed on April 1st of this year owing to
lack of funds. During February of this year he was a prominent
speaker at Russian meetings held in the American (Naval) Y. M. C.
A., Avenue Edward VII, at which the necessity of appointing
new officials in place of the present Russian Consular Officials

Secretary of the Y. M. C. A. gave a warning that the use of
the building would be discontinued, if political matters were
discussed.

Matveef left here for Vladivostock about four months ago
and attached is a translation from the Shanghai Life of 27th
March reporting a statement made by him to the Naval and Mili-
tary Authorities at Vladivostock as to the hostility displayed
towards Russians by foreigners in Shanghai, and advocating the
establishment of friendly relations with the Chinese.

Mr. Matveef Bodroy, ex-President of the Russian
Employment Bureau in Shanghai, has made a statement
concerning the position of Russians in Shanghai

are hostile to Russians, and do everything within
their power to restrict their activities. The
Chinese are the only people in Shanghai who
sympathize with Russians, and Matveef Bodroy
advised the immediate establishment of friendly
relations with the Chinese people who were
Russia's only friends in the Far East. The
foreign press in Shanghai had advocated that
the Police close the Russian Employment Bureau.
The Naval and Military Authorities were greatly
impressed by Mr. Matveef Bodroy's statement.

Made by D. I. Givens Forwarded by Chief Detective Officer.
Sir,
Some seventy Russians held a meeting in the
Russian Consulate at 6 p.m. 18th instant to emphasize a
protest which they had already made against an order
from the Orthodox Bishop in Peking dismissing the present
incumbent of the local Russian Church, who is a secular
priest, and replacing him by a monk. A Mr. Moeroff
presided and Mr. Ivanoff was present on behalf of the
Russian Consulate. The latter explained that the
Consulate had locked up the church pending the settlement
of the dispute, in accordance with instructions from
the Russian Ambassador. A discussion then took place
as to the steps which should be taken to ensure the
re-opening of the church and the retention of the present
priest, and it was finally decided to send a telegram
to the Russian Ambassador in Peking requesting him to
make an order to have the church re-opened, and to request
the Bishop to explain his reasons for dismissing the secular
priest. The discussion, in which Messrs. Lupovoi and
Zvereff were the principal participants lasted till 8 p.m.
when the meeting adjourned for three days.
The S. S. " Simbirsk " of the Russian Volunteer
Fleet arrived from Vladivostock on the afternoon of 18th
instant with one hundred and fifty five passengers,
including 106 Chinese, 6 Czecho- Slovacs, 9 Poles, and
2 Latvians. Ninety eight of the Chinese travelled
steerage.

Sir,

Some three hundred and fifty Russians attended a concert in the Chinese Y. M. C. A. on Szechuen Road on the evening of 15th instant which was held under the auspices of the Russian Employment Bureau in celebration of the Russian revolution, the anniversary of the outbreak of which occurred on 13th instant.

The curtain was raised at 9.30 p.m. when Mr. Smolensky, who was supported on the stage by Messrs. Budnewech, Mitauer, Kaufmann and Wolin, made a speech explaining that the political side of the programme had to be abandoned owing to the opposition of the local authorities. The Municipal Council had demanded that copies of the speeches to be delivered be submitted to it beforehand, but the organizers of the function had refused to submit to this indignity. A protest against the action of the Municipal Council would be sent to the new government in Vladivostock and the Russian Ambassador in Peking.

Mr. Semeschov then introduced General Potarov to the audience. He said all present were proud to have such a distinguished soldier among them that evening. He then mentioned amidst general applause that General Potanov was the first to raise the red flag in the Guard regiments. In thanking the audience for the reception accorded him, the General said the present rulers of Russia were denounced as murderers and criminals. The

ANNIVERSAIRE DE LA
RÉVOLUTION RUSSE

Les journalistes n'ont pas de chance... Un journal russe traite sévèrement le "Journal de Paris" parce que cet organe a refusé d'insérer le nom de Koltchak et un autre groupe russe en dit autant des journaux de Shanghai sur ses rétrogrades pour prier la police d'ouvrir l'œil sur les rouges de cette ville. Il veut bien admettre que la mise à mort du malheureux Nicolas II n'est pas un événement à rappeler aux masses, et là, nous sommes tout à fait de son avis, mais l'"Echo de Chine" qui fait partie des vendus dont parle notre confrère, est aussi d'avis que la présence à Shanghai de gens assez barbares pour approuver des actes de ce genre, est désagréable.

Ces apôtres de la liberté sont les glorificateurs du régime qui causa la ruine d'un grand nombre de Français en Russie et la mort de quelques-uns; d'un régime qui obligea la Russie à se parjurer en abandonnant ses Alliés pour soutenir l'Allemagne et renia les dettes de sa nation dont il détruisit ainsi le crédit, et c'est en songeant aux monceaux de cadavres et de ruines accumulés par lui que nous disons à la police de surveiller les approbateurs de ce régime.

Les Russes "démocrates" dans un journal local, parlent des partisans de l'ancien régime comme de valets etc... donnant ainsi raison aux paisibles citoyens et à la presse alliée qui croient une collusion possible entre les rouges et les blancs, et qu'ils ont été appelés vendus encore une fois, nous répétons qu'en autorisant une réunion du genre de celle d'hier au centre de Shanghai, le Municipal Council a commis une grave imprudence et a donné aux éléments extrémistes de la colonie russe une occasion de fusionner sous un

même drapeau. C'est là un effet déplorable sur les masses de la population chinoise qui ne demandent qu'à voir les étrangers s'entre-déchirer pour mieux les chasser ensuite du Municipal Council.

Shanghai est une ville internationale, c'est entendu, mais la liberté doit avoir des limites, et quelques uns doivent se souvenir que lorsqu'elle nuit à celle de la communauté, on la supprime. L'incident d'hier constitue un précédent autorisant les Allemands à fêter l'anniversaire du torpillage du "Lusitania"; les Britanniques n'admettront pas ces manifestations sans protester vigoureusement et notre paisible cité deviendra un enfer jusqu'au jour où les édiles de la concession internationale se verront obligés de passer d'un extrême à l'autre et de s'opposer à toutes les manifestations publiques, y compris la célébration des fêtes nationales.

Notre petite concession se gouvernant elle-même, est à l'abri de tels ennuis et les rouges de Shanghai savent qu'on y tolère pas les "non sens", c'est pourquoi, tout en l'habitant, ils font leur propagande ailleurs.

En admettant que rien d'extraordinaire ne se soit produit à la petite fête révolutionnaire organisée dans les locaux de la Y.M.C.A. de Szechuen Road, le précédent est quand même fâcheux; il fait une machine malsaine à un régime que les amis de l'ordre et de la paix exècrent du fond du cœur. Nous ne voyons qu'un seul avantage à la réunion démocratique d'hier soir, c'est d'avoir fourni aux détectives l'occasion de reconnaître certains assistants pour les mieux surveiller à l'avenir.

THE OTHER RUSSIANS IN
CHINA.
To the Editor of the
"NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS."
SIR,—I trust that you will not
refuse to publish in your columns
as soon as possible the following
address which it had been my
intention to deliver to the meet-
ing held on the 15th instant at
the Russian Workers' Bureau. The
meeting was called, by its organ-
isers, in the name of the Russian
Colony of Shanghai; but in spite
of this, and of the existing free-
dom of speech in Russia, that
meeting did not extend to me the
possibility of pronouncing my
opinions.
"To me, and I think to all at
the present meeting, it would be
very interesting to know upon
what authority and under instruc-
tions of what government you con-
sider yourselves entitled to decide
questions concerning the introduc-
tion of a control over the Russo-
Asiatic Bank and the Russian
Consulate-General in Shanghai.
No government has given you any
such orders and it would be diffi-
cult to imagine that any govern-
ment could give similar instruc-
tions to a mere handful of peo-
ple, 90 per cent. of whom are
entirely unknown to the real
Russian colony of Shanghai and
are favoured with no popularity
whatever by that latter body.
"Together the Russian residents
of Shanghai at the present time
total some three to four thousand
people. At this meeting are pre-
sent not more than 160 people,
among whom one may hardly count
more than 15 permanent residents.
Moreover, of those present only
50 or 60 have taken part in the
voting, the others have held back
and confined themselves solely to
listening to the words of the
orators. In what manner, then,
can this meeting consider itself
a legal interpreter of the desires
of the whole Russian colony?
"No, citizens, the present meet-
ing cannot adopt any resolution
in the name of the Russian Colony,
nor can any election carried out
by the meeting be recognized as
legal. It is not even our business
to decide such questions. I pre-
sume that the Russian Govern-
ment, without our assistance, will
decide the question of its diplo-
matic and consular representation
abroad. If the Government desires
to hear the opinions of the local
colony upon such matters it will
itself assemble the latter and give
them intimation.
"To us, it remains only to fol-
low attentively events taking place
at Home, and to wish for the
quickened advance of peace and
tranquility in the land of our
birth which has for three years
borne all the horrors of interne-
cine strife and has been watered
with the blood of our brothers. I
cannot, therefore, do otherwise
than join wholeheartedly with the
words of Mr. J. P. Tarasoff, who
has said plainly that here is no
place for the making of such de-
cisions, and that those who wish
to engage in politics must go
back to Russia."
Thanking you in advance for
your kindness,
I am, etc.,
L. J. LUGOVOI.
Shanghai, Feb. 17.

Made by D. S. I. Givens Forwarded by Chief Detective Officer.

Sir,

A meeting at which about a hundred Russians were present was held in the Russian Employment Bureau in the American (Naval) Y. M. C. A. at 5 p.m. 15th instant for the purpose of discussing the formation of a committee to take over the control of the Russian Consulates and branches of the Russo-Asiatic Bank in China.

Dr. Ginston, who was moved to the chair, made a short speech outlining the purpose of the meeting. He invited all persons who had suggestions to make as to how that purpose could best be attained to come forward and state their views.

Mr. Polejack responded to this invitation and proposed that the meeting should elect a committee of seven to call on the Consul General for Russia and the manager of the Russo-Asiatic Bank and demand that these establishments be placed under the committee's control. Several speakers had a heated discussion on the merits of this proposal, and it was finally dropped.

Mr. D. A. Lunden then took the platform and proceeded to address the gathering. Mr. Lunden felt that immediate steps should be taken to exercise control over the Russian Consulates and the various branches of the Russo-Asiatic Bank in China as there was very good reason to believe that the persons in charge of these concerns had entered into a conspiracy to convert government property and money to their own use. SHANGHAI TIMES, TUESDAY MARCH 23, 1920.
BOLSHEVIK PROPAGANDA IN CHINA
Agents At Work In Shanghai. In Touch With Disgruntled Politicians And Supposedly In French Concession.
A MAD DREAM OF WORLD CONQUEST

There is another interesting document in existence which shows that Trotzky, besides receiving a salary of Roubles 80,000 per month, is rapidly amassing a huge fortune. It is common knowledge that he has sent out to a bank in Argentine several million roubles in gold. When taxed by Lenin, Trotzky is said to have replied that he realises that the movement in Russia will fade away as rapidly as it had broken out, therefore he was going to make as much out of the "chance" as he could. These are the men that are intriguing for power in the Far East.

Campaign Opened in Earnest
There is overwhelming evidence that the Bolsheviks have opened their campaign in China in earnest. Many of their agents are staying in hotels in Hongkew and the French Concession. There is one man, who, we have every reason to believe, is directing the propaganda work in Shanghai, who lives in the French Concession. Of late he has been visited by several Chinese, some of them representing a student body, and one at least coming from a man who once was very popular, in fact a hero, in the eyes of the Chinese people. The callers in short, represent certain people who imagine they have a grievance against the central government or against the local Municipal Administration. It would seem, therefore, that the Bolsheviks are making a bid for the doubtful support of these malcontents. The Bolsheviks, who are past masters in the art of lying, will experience no difficulty in playing upon the feelings of these "water-brained" intriguers. Another frequent caller is a man who is connected with a local labour organisation.

This Russian who is attracting like a magnet the notorious disgruntled politicians in Shanghai, is evidently recruiting workers for the Bolshevik cause. There is a report that a printing plant has been established outside the Settlement which will turn out all the literature needed in the campaign in Shanghai. We have made exhaustive enquiries as to the location of the plant, and can only report that though many have been able, up to the present, to locate it, indications are not wanting that there is something in a secret place just beyond the Settlement that is drawing numbers of Russians at all hours of the day and night. The men directing the plant, or whatever it may be, live in Range Road and one of them travels to the place daily on a bicycle. It is said that he always goes out armed with a revolver.

Where Work Will First Start
The question has been frequently heard: Will the Bolsheviks succeed in winning the Chinese people over to their doctrine? They will not start their work among the intelligent and thinking classes, with whom they will find short shrift, unless, of course, these men are nursing grievances, imaginary or otherwise, against the Peking or the local Government. In that case the Bolsheviks will find the assistance which these men are able to render of great value. Where the Bolsheviks will first start their propaganda will be amongst coolies and the poor class of people who are mostly illiterate and ignorant. These are the people who will lend a willing ear to what the Bolsheviks will have to say. They become easy converts to Bolshevism.

Many Russians, who are believed to be agents of the Bolsheviks, can speak the Chinese language quite fluently. A number learnt the language through long residence in North China, others are the output of a school said to have been financed by the Bolsheviks at Harbin. There is a Russian journal here in Shanghai which has been exhibiting obvious pro-Bolshevik tendencies. In attempting to throw dust in the eyes of the Chinese Government, it one day declared that the Govern-

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, MONDAY, MARCH 22, 1920.

BOLSHEVIK PROPAGANDA IN CHINA

Plan Formulated As Long Ago As 1918: German Bankers
Pledge Fullest Financial Support

CAMPAIGN AGAINST BRITAIN IN CHINA & INDIA

(Specially Contributed To THE SHANGHAI TIMES).

There have appeared in the local press, from time to time, references to the presence of a certain class of Russians who are believed to be agents of the Bolsheviks. In some quarters, the report that the Bolsheviks in Shanghai are preparing a campaign affecting the whole of China is discredited. Let it be said here at the outset that the Bolsheviks are turning their eyes on the Asiatic continent, and that in doing so to-day, they are only carrying out a plan which had been formulated (in collaboration with the Germans) a couple of years ago. They are playing a big game, for they aim to convert no less than the 147 millions of Musulmans and the 400 millions of Chinese to their pernicious doctrine. They plan to seize the power of government in China, India and Japan. An ambitious plan, which, on the face of it, seems hardly likely to succeed. But the Bolsheviks have thought out a plan by which they hope to knock down the barrier of conservatism which hedges around the Chinese and the Japanese peoples. They will try first to create a small breach through which, by degrees, shall percolate the tenets of their doctrine.

The Master Mind

Their first plan was to reach India and China by way of the Caucasus, Turkestan and Afghanistan. Details of the plan had been closely discussed and settled as long ago as the year 1918. Needless to say, it was the German master mind which had thought out all the details for Lenin and Trotzky. These two latter were in the habit of receiving instructions from the German Minister of the Interior and from the notorious German Councillor von Truttmann. When Lenin had achieved his purpose in Russia and had secured the power of government, the Germans made him turn his eyes towards China and above all, India. The better known capitalists of Hamburg, who, for the most part were Jews, promised Lenin all the financial assistance he should need on condition that Jews in Russia were not molested and that their synagogues were respected.

The arrival of the Czecho-Slovaks in Siberia put a halt to the carrying out of this plan, but to-day, with Admiral Koltchak out of the way, with the Red army in occupation of practically the whole of Siberia, and the imminent secession of Vladivostok, with one of their own men, the bandit Krakowczky, in control of that port, the Bolsheviks are once more making an attempt to win over China and India to their doctrine.

The Influx Of Russians

The danger to China, more particularly, is very great. Within recent months there have filtered into Shanghai a large number of so-called Russians, who, though speaking the Russian language, are really not Russians at all. What are they doing in Shanghai? They cannot be looking for employment for there is hardly an opening for them here, and it is difficult to find work. Then why did they select Shanghai as their port of refuge? There can be but one explanation—they are here for no good purpose. In making this statement it is to be clearly understood that those true Russians who have suffered at the hands of the Bolsheviks and lost their all, are excluded. The so-called Russians who are here on behalf of the Bolsheviks are working in the dark, and the first opportunity they find to abuse the hospitality of the local authorities in permitting their sojourn here, they will seize it. Then will it be too late to think of measures to check them. Shanghai is knowingly nursing a snake in her bosom—a treacherous snake which will not hesitate to use its venomous fangs when the occasion arises. This will explain the explosion of hatred against the British in Hongkong who had refused to permit certain Russians to land, because the authorities were not sure of their bona fides.

Shanghai As Headquarters?
Is Shanghai going to be made the
general headquarters of Bolshevik
propaganda? It would seem so.
This old town of ours has
ever been, and always will be,
the headquarters from which dis-
gruntled politicians hatch and carry
out their intrigues against the
Government, a sort of haven of re-
fuge to political offenders of foreign
nations who find their native coun-
try a little unpleasant to live in for
the time being. It is only natural,
therefore, to expect that Shanghai
once more will be in the limelight as
the headquarters of Bolshevik pro-
paganda in the Far East. The only
remedy is to take the same steps
Shanghai took in the case of the
Germans: to chase them from the
town But this is hardly feasible
just yet. Public opinion has not yet
been sufficiently aroused.

Germany Financing Propaganda
Germany, from information in our
possession, is very deeply concerned
over the Bolshevik move in China
and India. She is supporting the
move with money and men. In
the year 1917, in the month of
March, a prominent German Bank
opened a credit in the names of
Lenin and Trotzky for use in their
propaganda work in China and
India. A special credit was also
opened in the name of Trotzky, by
a German banker of the name of
Bunstein, to wipe out the Christian
religion and the church in Russia, as
well as in Asia.
But the most interesting move in
the financing of the Bolsheviks by
the Germans was made on January
8, 1918, when the German Imperial
Bank, through von Schlantz, in-
formed Trotzky that a sum of 50,-
000,000 marks in gold had been
placed at his disposal at Stockholm
specially for use in connection with
Bolshevik propaganda in China and
India. In the document of instruc-

Schlantz counselled Trotzky and
Lenin to employ as many persons of
Jewish birth as they could.

Campaign Against Great Britain
Above all, von Schlantz impressed
upon Lenin and Trotzsky the import-
ance of undermining Great Bri-

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, WEDNESDAY, MARCH 17, 1920.

BOLSHEVIK
AGITATORS IN
SHANGHAI

It is gratifying to observe that the local Municipal authorities, with commendable wisdom, prohibited a certain section of Russian residents of Shanghai from celebrating the third anniversary of the assassination of the late Tsar NICHOLAS of Russia last Saturday with "political speech-making." In our issue of last Thursday, we pointed out that such a celebration was dangerous and out of place in this International Settlement and therefore, it is a matter of satisfaction to us that our advice was acted upon and the celebration suppressed. Instead of the threatened celebration, it appears that the local Bolsheviks indulged in the more innocuous pastime of a concert held on Monday night at the Chinese Y.M.C.A. with the permission of the Municipal Council, conditional on the promise that political speeches would not be made. Our Slavonic friends, we are told, now threaten to lodge a protest with the government at Vladivostock, setting forth that Russians in Shanghai are not allowed the "rights of other nationals who celebrate anniversaries of revolutions in their respective homelands." Doubtless, the self-appointed rulers at Vladivostock will duly issue a Ukase to the Shanghai Municipal Council, but inasmuch as the Vladivostock "government" has as yet no "locus standi," and is not likely to have one for some time to come, it is doubtful whether the Shanghai Municipal Council will "tremble and obey" at the behest of the amiable men at Vladivostock. The threat of such a protest is puerile in the extreme. Shanghai is not Soviet Russia, and if local Russians wish to continue enjoying the hospitality of the Settlement, they will have to abide by the laws and regulations of the place. They dare not run counter to foreign public sentiment here, which is dead against any attempt to disseminate in Shanghai the dirty creed of Bolshevism. The proper place to extol murder and outrage is Soviet Russia, not Shanghai. If the local Bolsheviks wish to enjoy that liberty which enables them to belaud cold-blooded butchery, they will find every freedom in this respect in that part of unhappy Russia controlled by the Bolsheviks. Let them go there and enjoy to their heart's content the brand of freedom they appear to admire. We can truthfully assure them they will not be missed from Shanghai. We have been reading a curious screed by a Chinese vernacular paper on the subject of Bolshevism as it may or may not affect China. The journal in question argues that there is no occasion to fear the successful dissemination of Bolshevism in China and in support of its contention advances the following proposals: "Firstly, the Government should respect the freedom of opinions and expressions. It should let the people alone in studying all sorts of 'isms' or doctrines, and in the discussion, writing and publication of the like. This measure is the best means to moderate revolutions. If free and open discussion is allowed, it will give the people chances to study the truth as well as the fallacies of the various sorts of 'isms' or theories, and will develop in them the ability and soundness of judgment which will naturally restrain them from foolish and immature actions. In England, class struggle is very severe, but the country is free of revolutions. It is benefitted by the system of free discussions. Therefore we do not consider the dissemination of Bolshevism in China a serious question at all. Because dissemination necessarily involves discussion; and discussion produces judgment. If the peoples' ability of judgment is sound, no evil will result from Bolshevism's dissemination. Then why should we be scared of it?" The scribe who penned the above overlooks the fact that the Chinese people are not so politically advanced as to render harmless the dissemination and discussion of the Bolshevik creed. The situation in China is hardly analogous with that of Great Britain or other politically progressive countries, and in the hands of unscrupulous alien agitators, the Chinese would prove very pliable tools for the furtherance of the interests of men who are devoid of morals principles or religion. The Bolsheviks in Shanghai are hugging a delusion if they cherish the ambition of converting the International Settlement of Shanghai into a centre for their machinations and espionage to the end of creating an eventual disturbance of our normal life. They have to choose between one of two things—either they have to mend their manners or they will face instant deportation. We have deported the Germans and Austrians from China. We shall not hesitate to deport the Bolsheviks in Shanghai, as they constitute a potential danger to the community not a whit less than the Germans and Austrians.
